title: Unit Econ Driver Modeling Notes (batching, caching, quantization) — hypotheses for post-launch validation
content:
Context
- This doc is a working set of hypotheses connecting runtime levers (batching, caching, quantization profiles) to the canonical dashboard KPI: blended_cost_usd_per_1m_output_tokens (aka “blended $/1M output tokens”).
- Primary use: after the internal unit-econ dashboard lands, we need a shared mental model for (a) what should move the metric and (b) what attribution we expect the “Explain cost delta” panel to surface.
- This is not the formal metric definition (see ADR + data contracts). This is a driver model and validation plan.

Definitions (informal, for reasoning)
- Let:
  - C_total = total blended cost allocated to serving over time window (compute + overhead allocation; excluding/including discounts per Finance definition)
  - T_out = total output tokens over time window
  - KPI = 1e6 * C_total / T_out
- For a slice (model, region, tier, runtime_config), KPI_slice = 1e6 * C_slice / T_out_slice
- We expect the biggest drivers to appear via:
  - (1) throughput (tokens/sec per GPU) changes → C_total changes for same T_out
  - (2) cache avoidance (served tokens that don’t require full compute) → C_total changes and/or T_out changes depending on how we count cached tokens
  - (3) mix shifts (more traffic on expensive model/region/tier) → KPI changes even if each slice is stable

Key model: KPI decomposition we want
We want an “Explain” decomposition that can attribute week-over-week delta in KPI into:
1) Mix shift (composition):
   - model mix (share of tokens by model family/variant)
   - region mix (share of tokens by region)
   - tier mix (self_serve vs dedicated vs private vs enterprise)
   - runtime_config mix (batching/caching/quant profile adoption)
2) Within-slice efficiency:
   - per-slice cost changes (GPU price inputs, overhead allocation changes, efficiency regressions)
   - per-slice output token accounting changes (metering changes, tokenizer/model version changes)

The levers below primarily act through “within-slice efficiency” but will also appear as a runtime_config mix shift as adoption ramps.

A. Batching (continuous batching / dynamic batching)
Hypothesis A1: Increased effective batch size reduces KPI by increasing tokens/sec per GPU at the same p95 latency budget.
- Mechanism: higher GPU utilization, better kernel occupancy, amortized overhead per request.
- Expected dashboard signature:
  - KPI down for slices with higher avg_batch_size / higher concurrent_inflight.
  - Compute-cost-per-output-token down; overhead allocation per token may also trend down if overhead is allocated proportional to compute spend.
- Guardrails:
  - Latency SLO: more batching can increase time-to-first-token (TTFT) and tail latency.
  - Dedicated tiers: may already run “hotter”; incremental gains lower vs self_serve.

Hypothesis A2: There is a “batching sweet spot” by model + sequence length distribution; beyond it, KPI improvements plateau or reverse.
- Mechanism: KV cache memory pressure and fragmentation, scheduler overhead, more preemption, and/or higher queueing delay → less throughput.
- Expected signature:
  - KPI improvements flatten as avg_batch_size increases past threshold; p95 latency increases.
  - Region variance: smaller regions with less traffic may not reach stable batch sizes; KPI higher and more volatile.

What to validate post-launch (batching)
- Correlate KPI_slice vs:
  - avg_batch_size (or effective_batch_tokens)
  - queue_time_ms / scheduler_delay
  - tokens_per_second_per_gpu (if we can compute from telemetry)
- Suggested analysis view:
  - scatter plot: KPI vs avg_batch_size by model family (color), with p95 latency (size)
  - time series: adoption of batching profile → KPI change, controlling for model mix

Instrumentation / dimensions needed
- runtime_config (batching profile name/version)
- avg_batch_size and/or avg_inflight
- latency breakdown: queue_time vs compute_time (to separate “more batching” vs “more waiting”)

Open questions (batching)
- Do we want to standardize a “batch efficiency index” per slice? Something like tokens/sec per GPU normalized by sequence length.
- For the unit-econ pipeline, do we store avg_batch_size at daily grain or only as supporting stats in a separate table to avoid cardinality blow-ups?


B. Caching (prefix cache / KV cache reuse)
Hypothesis B1: Higher cache hit rate reduces KPI by lowering compute cost per output token, even if billed output tokens are unchanged.
- Mechanism: cached prefixes reduce prefill compute; KV reuse reduces attention cost.
- Expected signature:
  - KPI down as prefix_hit_rate / kv_reuse_rate goes up.
  - “Estimated cache savings” field (ENG-2913 / PR-11884) should explain most of delta during cache rollouts.

Important nuance: how KPI counts tokens when cache hits occur
- We need consistency between:
  - what’s counted in T_out (output tokens returned)
  - what’s counted in cost attribution (compute actually consumed)
- In most caching scenarios, output tokens are still generated (decode) but prefill cost is reduced.
- Therefore KPI should generally decrease because C_total goes down while T_out is stable.

Hypothesis B2: Cache hit rate effect is nonlinear; benefits are larger for longer prompts and higher prompt repetition.
- Mechanism: saved prefill tokens scale with prompt length.
- Expected signature:
  - KPI improvements concentrate in workloads with high avg_prompt_tokens and high repetition.
  - Model differences: models with more expensive prefill (architectural/kernel differences) see larger savings.

Hypothesis B3: Cache systems can “move cost around” (compute → memory/infra overhead), which may partially offset KPI gains depending on overhead allocation.
- Mechanism: additional cache memory footprint, cache coordination services, increased network traffic.
- Expected signature:
  - Compute component down but overhead component may tick up; net KPI improvement depends on allocation rules.
  - Potential region effects where cache infra is priced differently.

What to validate post-launch (caching)
- Create a weekly view for:
  - prefix_hit_rate, kv_hit_rate (or equivalent)
  - estimated_cache_usd_saved
  - KPI and compute_usd_per_1m_output_tokens (if we expose cost components)
- Run a difference-in-differences analysis around cache rollout flags by region:
  - treatment regions where cache enabled vs control
  - hold model and tier constant

Instrumentation / dimensions needed
- cache_policy_id and cache_enabled boolean
- prefix_hit_rate, kv_reuse_rate (daily aggregated)
- estimated cache savings methodology doc link embedded in dashboard (so Finance/PMs don’t misread it as invoiced savings)

Open questions (caching)
- Do we need separate fields for “saved prefill tokens” vs “saved compute seconds” for auditability?
- How to handle late-arriving cache telemetry? (We’ve seen variance spikes when cache metrics land late.)


C. Quantization profiles (e.g., FP16 → INT8/INT4 variants)
Hypothesis C1: Quantization adoption decreases KPI by increasing tokens/sec per GPU and/or reducing GPU count needed for the same throughput.
- Mechanism: faster matmuls, lower memory bandwidth pressure; higher batch feasibility due to smaller KV/weights.
- Expected signature:
  - KPI drops for slices where quantization_profile != baseline.
  - Additional second-order effect: better batching + less OOM → improved utilization.

Hypothesis C2: Quantization savings are largest for memory-bound models and long-context workloads.
- Mechanism: smaller weights/KV reduce memory traffic; decode loop may become compute-bound.
- Expected signature:
  - Larger KPI deltas for long context distributions, or when avg_seq_len is high.

Hypothesis C3: Quantization can increase “waste” if it triggers quality regressions and customers compensate with longer prompts / more retries.
- Mechanism:
  - More retries or longer outputs increase T_out and/or request count; might raise costs even if per-token compute is cheaper.
- Expected signature:
  - KPI may improve while customer-perceived cost (invoice) or application-level cost might worsen (more tokens per task).
  - Need to watch request-level stats: avg_output_tokens/request, retry rate, fallback rate.

What to validate post-launch (quant)
- Quant profile adoption tracker joined to unit econ slices (ENG-2912 / PR-11863):
  - adoption_rate = tokens on quant_profile / total tokens for model+region
- Compare KPI for same model+region+tier across quant_profile values.
- Add an “impact sanity check”:
  - does p95 latency improve?
  - do error rates / fallback rates change?
  - does avg_output_tokens/request move?

Instrumentation / dimensions needed
- quantization_profile (stable string + version)
- runtime_config_version (so we can distinguish kernel/runtime changes from quant itself)
- fallback_model_used boolean (graceful degradation can hide failures but impact cost)

Open questions (quant)
- How do we represent “hybrid” scenarios (prefill quantized, decode not; or partial layers) without exploding cardinality?
- Do we need a “quality guardrail” annotation in the dashboard when a quant profile is known to affect certain evals?


D. Cross-effects (these levers interact)
Hypothesis D1: Quantization increases batching headroom → multiplicative savings.
- Model: quant reduces per-request memory footprint; scheduler can pack more sequences.
- Expected signature: quant rollout correlates with both avg_batch_size increase and KPI decrease; attribution should avoid double-counting.

Hypothesis D2: Caching reduces prefill compute which can reduce the “available batching signal” (less work to batch), potentially increasing variance.
- For some workloads, prefill becomes less dominant; decode dominates and batching gains are smaller.

Hypothesis D3: “Optimization” can shift the limiting resource (GPU → network/CPU) and show up as overhead, not compute.
- We need overhead breakouts (or at least notes) so teams don’t assume GPU-side changes explain all KPI movement.


E. Practical driver model for the dashboard (what we want the UI to say)
When KPI moves, we want the dashboard to answer:
1) Did KPI move because traffic moved to a different mix? (model/region/tier)
2) For the big slices, did KPI move because:
   - batching efficiency changed?
   - cache hit rate changed?
   - quantization adoption changed?
   - underlying GPU $/hour or allocation changed?
3) Is the movement “real” or data quality / reconciliation artifact?

Proposed “driver fields” to prioritize in V1 explain panel
- Mix:
  - model_family_share, region_share, tier_share
- Efficiency:
  - avg_batch_size (or effective_batch_tokens)
  - cache_hit_rate (prefix and/or kv)
  - quantization_profile adoption rate
  - tokens_per_gpu_second (if available)
- Data quality:
  - freshness lag indicator
  - reconciliation variance indicator (billing vs unit-econ)


F. Validation plan (first 4 weeks post-launch)
Week 1: Baseline sanity
- Confirm KPI totals reconcile within tolerance.
- Establish baseline correlations (KPI vs model mix, region mix) to avoid misattributing obvious mix shifts to optimizations.

Week 2: First lever deep-dive (caching)
- Identify top 3 regions by token volume with meaningful cache adoption.
- Quantify KPI change explained by cache_savings_estimate.
- Confirm no major increase in overhead allocation masking savings.

Week 3: Second lever deep-dive (batching)
- Compare KPI across runtime_config batching profiles.
- Look for p95 latency regressions; confirm whether we’re “buying” KPI improvements with worse tail latency.

Week 4: Third lever deep-dive (quant)
- Compare KPI on baseline vs quantized profiles for 1–2 model families.
- Add notes on any observed changes to fallback rate / output tokens per request.


Notes / risks
- Cardinality risk: if runtime_config is too granular (includes hash-like values), we will not be able to slice safely. We need a curated runtime_config_label.
- Attribution risk: overlapping rollouts (cache + quant + batching) will make simplistic attribution misleading. We should expect to use controlled experiments where possible (staged region rollout) and rely on mix-shift decomposition + within-slice deltas.
- Finance interpretation risk: “cache savings estimate” is not the same as invoiced savings if billing is not aligned to compute saved. We should label it explicitly as an internal cost attribution estimate.

Action items
- (Aditya) Draft a short “expected driver impacts” cheat sheet for Finance/Product weekly review so they know what patterns to look for.
- (Logan/Nadia) Confirm which supporting fields will be in the semantic layer at daily grain without cardinality blowups (avg_batch_size, cache hit, quant_profile).
- (Arjun/Jonas) Provide a stable quantization_profile taxonomy + versioning guidance; list planned rollouts by region/model so we can pick clean before/after windows.
- (Thomas) Propose a runtime_config labeling scheme that’s human-readable and stable across deployments.

Appendix: quick mental math examples (for narrative alignment)
1) Batching improvement example
- If tokens/sec per GPU improves by 15% for a slice and demand is fixed, we expect GPU-hours to drop ~13% (1/1.15) for that slice.
- KPI should drop ~13% for that slice, assuming overhead is proportional.

2) Caching improvement example
- If prefill compute is 30% of total compute and caching cuts prefill compute by half for 40% of requests, then compute reduction ≈ 0.30 * 0.50 * 0.40 = 6%.
- KPI impact may look “small” unless prompt repetition is high; this helps set expectations.

3) Quantization + batching interaction example
- Quant alone yields 10% throughput improvement, but also allows 10% higher avg_batch_size which yields another 8% throughput improvement.
- Net throughput ≈ 1.10 * 1.08 = 1.188 → ~16% cost reduction if demand fixed.
- Attribution should avoid claiming 10% + 8% independently without acknowledging interaction.
